text: TWILIGHT SITTING 2026-09-26: THE TOP-THREE FRAMING IS REJECTED AND REPLACED BY A BETTER MECHANIC. Owner typed the above. What it establishes: (a) A SKYLIGHT DRIFTS OVER ABOUT A WEEK, not over years as the frozen sheet and both design passes assumed. That is a playable cadence a colony actually experiences, not background lore. It supersedes the sheet's 'every light-well is temporary on a years scale' timing while leaving hard ban 5 (no permanent skylight) intact. (b) THERE ARE OTHER LIGHTS THE PLAYER GROWS SLOWLY THEMSELVES - the sun-sphere / ollumin culture line. (c) 🔑 THE LOAD-BEARING INSIGHT, his: 'and this explains the movable chained floating fields.' The tethered cage farms are movable BECAUSE the light moves. Chain a floating field and walk it to follow the drifting shaft, or culture your own light and stay put. That fuses two previously separate ideas into one trade and gives the biome its arc: early game you chase the light, late game you make it and become independent of the Compact's leases. (d) It also DISSOLVES a conflict the review sheet had filed as its own row - 'the sun-sphere frees the player from the skylight economy' vs 'skylight tenancy is the #1 marquee'. Not a conflict: that IS the progression. (e) A week-long drift also rescales skylight tenancy: a Compact lease is short-term and renewed, not generational. ⇒ NO ranked top three. He asked to 'explore the others more dynamically' - the remaining four (dry river as travel lane, the gardener's events, living light, charts and ledgers) are open for design, not queued behind a fixed 1-2-3.

title: The bedazzle program: eleven biomes raised to the Baroque bar in ruled order (Contagion first, Black Crags last), four-movement ritual, nine-mark bar as the design gate; all other biomes grandfathered subject to the gate
ownerSaid: Bedazzle means we take what's there and review, fill the flora/fauna roster, then start ideating what could be REALLY awesome/unique mechanics. text: Owner's authoritative history of ExplosiveGrowth intent; next: consensus review.
ownerSaid: To be clear: the original design was simply me saying the dry-adapted alien plants of this world generally barely grow at all until they get access to water, then they grow x10 speed to take advantage of it. That's what I originally meant by explosive growth. You heard that and misinterpreted it to mean they actually detonate, and I thought that was fascinating as a concept. So we accepted the exploratory idea that the plants grow and grow until at peak maturity they sometimes burst/die, resulting in many additional sprouts surrounding them. This was later adapted to a reduced growth factor in permanently wet areas and making fruit instead of bursting. I hope that clarifies the discussion that's been happening. Now we need to do a review of what's been planned and implemented here to bring everyone into consensus together.

text: Owner rulings 2026-10-18 card: (1) shallow drowning stays default-on. ownerSaid: Drown slowly, keep default [shallows drowning stays on]. PIT ROOM: the superdeep came from the observation that a human can lift their arms up and pull themselves out of a pit. It needs to be deep enough that an athletic human could not reasonably raise their arms over their head and jump a little to grab the edge, then scramble up the side. Use that rule to determine. PAINTED PONDS: if the source is effectively infinite (huge in map, or extends off map, or a river) then it does not get a sloped floor. We should stick with that. We will work out appearance matching later. HOSE LEFTOVER: yes, and it's not just filth, it's spilled water as per wetting the ground, plant growth, etc.

ownerSaid: Let's talk about this. A very large creature (say 10 cell) may see a narrow slot in a wall as 'something way down there, I don't care' and simply walk over a wall, damaging the wall as though it were an object. This would not be true of a thin passage through a mountain. If a large creature is trapped by thin wooden walls around it, it walks through them effortlessly; if the walls were as thick as it is, no longer. I like squeezing through logic if at least half its width: slowing, not a stop. Do a design pass for the options so we can have different ideas for maximum game fun. Do a GPT review of your idea. Likely also involves whether the building is roofed or not: a free-standing thin unroofed wall is easier to smash than a roofed one.

This should allow pawns to scale walls (unroofed on both sides) just as easily as canal sides, albeit slowly. Then jump packs and other leaping abilities allow entrance/exit immediately, and teleportation, etc.

Please commission that as art and as a review sheet item to watch work.

And there should be a debug/god-mode click button to force open or closed. Your art for "open" is wrong: it never opens. ownerSaid: Suspension: 2 or 3 (towers should be VERY expensive to build, so using islands is important for resource savings). Drawbridges: A: one drag. Dig/fill: And of course you can't dig in sand or mud (just slides back in). Do a brief analysis of Rimworld to see if there are other kinds of ground we might have to worry about. The gravel (broken rock) that it produces should be able to satisfy some recipies for items that might otherwise consume blocks or chunks (if they get melted down, for example). title: GSS rebuilds a whole-map CordWorld snapshot (CordWorldAdapter.cs:21) on every Terrain/Buildings dirty (MapMeshDirty prefix RM_MapComponent_CordGraph.cs:911); basin digging may cost O(map cells + edges) per frame on 325 maps. Measure; fix = incremental snapshot patching changed cells

why: Offline read 2026-10-26: GSS does NOT share the hose's paused per-frame O(N^2) choke (static SectionLayer print, once-per-frame change-driven Rebuild:200, per-edge cache CordBuilder.cs:150-225, view-culled capped batched motion DrawMotion:608). The one shared term is the full-map snapshot per change, the same as hose World():139. Recipe: 325 map, E=0/50/200/800 cord edges; paused frame mean/p99 over 300 frames on and off screen; at 3x with a pawn digging a basin of about 200 cells, Builds/s and LastRebuildMs; one conduit placed, LastPlanned vs LastReused. Pass: paused flat in E, rebuild under 16 ms, dig adds under 10% frame time. Fix if it fails: patch the changed cells into the snapshot (detect them as hose CellChanged:209 does) instead of Snapshot(map)

title: Evaluate owner's three-agent design (Conductor + FOUNDRY with Ralph builder/critic subagents + TestPilot live tester that fixes in-session, reloads only on burden of proof) against the architecture zoo; independent Opus and GPT passes, cross-response, merge; simulate
ownerSaid: I think I'm ready. I just want us to inherit s much oh style wisdom as possible. Right now I'm thinking one agent should focus entirely on live testing debugging and fixing all at once. NOT writing out findings for later fixing but doing them right there while the context is fresh and perhaps even being able to continue testing if it's something that could be hot loaded into the game like savegame modification or bridge injected testing structure to improve. Testing scenario. Massively accelerated live game testing. Only if it has no useful valid live tests temaining to conduct would it suffer a reload. Optimization metrics would be how swiftly it can execute live tests, avoid loss of live game time, and use subagents to build fixes while it continued the live testing past dilutes where possible. Intelligence would be required to evaluate if follow in tests remain viable after a failure. The intention would be to detect additional unrelated bugs while still having the game live to minimize reload after every failure. Essentially there would be a Burden of proof required to trigger a reload. Then there would be a two faced builder ralph as subagents of. Foundry. By that I mean one Ralph subagent would do nothing but build items in classic Ralph loop style. Then foundry would pass those items to a highly skeptical blind subagent tester trying to break and criticise, and only when passing them back and forth between fresh blind builder and critique subagents would the foundry instance call it done. Then they go to the live tester.  The live tester can refuse the evidence and pass it back for improvement or crept it and build a testing plan. The live tester would spend its time during game reload writing testing plans for new items and sending them off for critical review (both testing plan and code together), and if they both get accepted, then it goes through the live testing and fixing. Only in the event of catastrophic mismatch with live game would it send it back to foundry, say if the design spec had to be radically modified. That would be a conductor decision for now and really shouldnt happen much. So I guess I'm describing foundry, testpilot, and conductor as a three gent system that fundamentally uses subagents ti get thing done. Please evaluate this proposal finer the other options in our growing zoo of architectures. Do. Deep designpass to see how it might fit in simulation nd get realistic critiques in it. Thanks. Opus nd gpt both then merge findings after plowing each to respond nd improve or defend their design. Allow  them to say critical problem with their own design nd improve it if offered.

The mod isn't handed to a Relentless worker until this tree is well defined. It shouldn't attempt to define EVERYTHING, just the core concepts that must be true for the mod to pass. They should appear to host many of the other lines plugging into the power strips and connectors, as the means to join the many cables. Cables should look messy and only loosely follow the conduit in the floor. It should not repeat patterns but appear like real messy cables strewn across the floor. Cables should pile against the wall, resist tight turns, and tend toward gently curving tangles and coils. The point is to make the game look more realistic and support the experience of scavengers, sloppy junkers, and trailer trash. The four kinds of art are intended to support different game styles. text: Owner ruling 2026-11-04 on the Test Pilot's scope; written into .claude/agents/rm-testpilot.md and testpilot_route.brief()
ownerSaid: Recall we were deciding on the rules when a test pilot is called in to debug active testing, be more free firm in its investigation of alive game, capable of filing tickets about strange things beyond its specified checklist items in a similar way that as humans expectations might react to the game, and tries to "make something productive" come from a live test even if it needs to get creative or diagnose the test itself rather than the mod code. Might even be able to test additional functionality beyond instruction like "well the pit is filled with water, but let's make sure people can still swim there…" like a human tester would.

text: Owner ruling 2026-11-04: Test Pilot's core job is MEASURING SURPRISE. Built at 1107f01a89: rm-testpilot.md section + testpilot_route.brief() LOOK cadence (start/each experiment/~10 min), monitor = jawa/vitals (self-described test-state monitor), capture = system_screenshot.py + jawa/take_screenshot, modal list before clear_ui, EXPECTED/ODD/ALARMING scores, TESTPILOT_SAT surprises field; selftest_testpilot_route green.
ownerSaid: I would also like the test pilot to be very visually focused. While it can of course use bridge to know the underpinnings if the game and should, it should regularly "look at" the screen and reason about what it's seeing. Does it make sense to see the beasts displayed in this biome? Are there inexplicable dead animals or colonists everywhere and a mechanoid wandering around? Looking at the game state monitor can help here too. Is there fire outside of a fire test? Are there merchants or raiders? Is there a modal dialog in the screen? Things like that. Context. It should be given latitude to gather context and then reason about how surprising any of it is. That's what's the test pilot is really about. Measuring surprise.

title: Test Pilot surprise book: explain-away before filing, retire boring surprise per context, revive on a real bug
ownerSaid: I really like the surprise angle. And when it finds what seems surprising (omg there are mushrooms everywhere) it then has a chance to prove it's not surprising (oh, this is the rot biome, that makes sense) or (oh this is the… desert? That's not right!) might require building some kind of context about what is surprising. If it keeps thinking boring things are surprising we will need to retire some surprise. Make sense? This can be the agent learning.

title: FireHawk review: his eight verdicts go into the flying art skill, then one offline fix attempt (east double wing, eyes level)
ownerSaid: A: North and south look good. East was built from a version with a static wing in the "down" position along the body, so as the wing flaps you see two wings: the moving one, and the "down" one at the same time. There's also something wrong with the wing when it's pointed mostly at the camera, but it goes by so quickly I just see strange static-like noise where the problem is. B is nearly identical with the same problem, though the wings appear to beat more and that's better. Bird C North has an unflapping right wing though I can see some of the right wing peeking into its lower right quadrant, likely just a graphic mapping error. East shows the same defect as above. Bird D has the body bobbing wildly and is quite silly, but I think maybe just adjusting it to keep the eyes level between shots might be the best fix we've got to get out of this terrible loop. Bird E is a chicken that satisfies the requirements perfectly. Bird F is nearly identical to Bird A. Bird G is terrifying! The wings have been morphed away from the body incorrectly, so some of the white flesh appears to rip away from the body in a horrific sliced-off-cartoonish way. Bird H looks like Bird A except it is now missing any art in the upper left North facing, and shows the same east defect as all the others. FireHawk review sheet bad news. Much of this needs to be put into the Rimworld art skill for flying.

title: Spring cleaning: extract and promote skills across agents, handoffs, memory and CLAUDE.md; artisan and Relentless especially; clean and repoint
ownerSaid: Please skillfully extract skills across all our agents, handoff files, processes, conventions, memory files, claude.md... everywhere. Look for opportunities to promote generalized skills out of RimMandrake to the broader user level as part of MandrakeWorkflows or as their own repo if relevant. Promote skills out of agents into shared skills that are reusable across the project. Remove redundancies, merge rather than concatenate, and move evidence into pointer history files while keeping the lessons themselves in the active files. Provenance is for git. Especially consider skills related to our artisan agentic work, possibly more than one, in terms of creating them, guiding them, monitoring them, the resources they benefit from, judging them, model usage, etc. Relentless pipeline is the same: there is likely much wisdom to pull into Relentless within mandrake workflows that isn't specific to RimMandrake. Consider our own claude.md in this project and whether generalized guidance should be moved into the Lodestar-managed user-level fragment system. Do this as a subagent. Comb through the handoff files and past conversations, extract what is useful. Clean any files no longer meaningful such as old handoff files. If files are pointing into handoff files and other unsafe practices, repoint them to lessons files or other distillations. Be thorough and make us clean and efficient! Spring cleaning time!

text: OWNER RULINGS 2026-11-08 ~1:10 PM PST (sitting): (1) strips and junctions carry NO pre-drawn cord stubs to join to; on large or non-our objects run the cord beneath to the object's base; on our own art draw a plug over the socket so our cord looks plugged in (power strips above all: one cable ends in the strip, others plug into it). (2) A cord may come from another cord only through a drawn junction box or power strip. (3) A cord leaves a plug straight; a high-stress bend right at the plug only where a wall or object forces it; else a tight wire-tied strain-relief loop just after the plug, or a right-angle plug, lets it leave at any angle (his GPT mockup: normal plug with natural bend radius / wire-tied loop / sideways plug). (4) Only his OneDrive Windows captures count; his two F10 shots were cursor-pointing attempts, not evidence.
ownerSaid: A general rule: power-strips and junctures should likely NOT have "pre-built wires sticking out of them" that we try to join to. They never look right and can't participate in the flexible drawing. Instead, we should either run the wires beneath objects (to their base) if the objects are large and especially if they aren't our art. If they are ours, however, showing a plug that gets "drawn over" to look precisely as it would if our coords "plugged into them" is far superior. This is especially true for power strips, where the whole point is cleverly making it look like one cable ends in a power strip that other cables plugged into. ... Splices: It is entirely acceptable for a cord to come from another cord, that is what junction boxes or power strips are for and would be drawn that way. Plug direction: Just like real wires, it is very hard for a wire to bend immediately after emerging from a plug. Only if the geometry absolutely requires it should it have that high-energy, high-stress bend (such as next to a wall or other object). To make it look more natural, it can sometimes be useful to add a tight LOOP there as though the installer wire-tied a small loop tightly just after the plug to allow the cable to come out at an arbitrary angle.

title: Every refusal by a judge or gate carries detail equal to the evidence, an attainable path to pass and an assessment of the acceptance criteria; flawed criteria go at once to a neutral fixer (not the judge), then the item is rejudged; 'nothing could ever pass' is an immediate alarm
ownerSaid: We MUST ensure that we don't get trapped letting poorly tuned Judges refuse everything forever, burning tokens, and providing no signal to improve upon. ANY refusals must be as detailed as the evidence they are rejecting and include the fixes and paths towards passing that are attainable and reasonable. It also MUST include assessment of the acceptance criteria themselves. If they are found to be flawed, we need a process to immediately bring a neutral fixer in to repair them independent of the Judge itself so as not to bias towards pass = success and repair the demonstrated flaws or insufficiencies. Evidence that "this item doesn't pass" is not valuable. Evidence that "nothing could ever pass" is grounds for immediate, swift action. Then the item is immediately rejudged once the acceptance criteria are repaired. Agreed? This is VITAL. No more repeated loops for the sake of ceremony! No more broken acceptance tests causing judges to destroy my account uselessly.

It would be useful to have it be textured the ground (varieties of mud) as well as have revealed aquatic plants that are dying or even stranded fish and creatures. How hard would that be? Could even be a great way to introduce some terrible beasts that were living in there and are none too happy that they are now suffocating to death thanks to your pumping. Also: how hard would it be to allow planting zones to be placed on the exposed ground? Finally, it would of course be \"wetted ground\" for quite awhile, but it seems like we would want it to be able to dry out, especially in the hot Ash'karr sun.

text: Owner's answer 2026-11-13 ~10:20 PST to the open Designer question walk_season_on_the_pyre ('what must a season's walk on the pyre show you before you call it right?'). Phone typo fixed: 'fight after a fire' -> 'right after a fire'.
ownerSaid: Full season on the Pyre (despite Utinni being a scenario of constant movement and never staying a season): The grass grows so swiftly, you only barely know what bare ash looks like save for right after a fire. Fire is always coming, you never should "wait for a calm stretch when you can..." The beasts start fires. You've seen it happen. The Furnace Beast. The Firehawk. Even the Lightning itself: the Pyrelands WANT to burn. The scorchfruit makes it worthwhile: rich abundance from the ashes, and your freezer stuffed if you're prepared with room. But then the Deep Tribes come: learning to watch rather than confront. Offer trade and leave them their share, and you'll be ok. The Black Ash rain: a violent time with violent plenty right after, and a rare chance to fill your moat against the fire and fill your water tanks. And I won't miss having to sweep the ash away from all my paths to keep walking clear, or the choking smoke that sometimes come as its own weather...

ownerSaid: So can we wire up Operations/Dispatch such that they do advance on these offline builders? This was pretty inefficient and pointlessly it seems, if I'm reading correctly. As long as we don't have automated loops rejecting/cycling things, we can't get into too much trouble.

text: Dispatch step now ticks every 60 s for page and launch decisions alike (timer OnUnitActiveSec=60s, dispatcher_schedule every_s 60, spec/plan/docstrings updated; reading dead-age alarm kept 30 min). New settle_s 180 guard: a run that ended under 180 s ago is not judged or relaunched. sha a63c87d50ccb. Waste of a 10-min launch wait would be up to 10 min per builder end; at 60 s it is under 4 min incl. settle.
ownerSaid: MATURATION NOW should be 60 seconds, yes, and it's ok to leave launch decisions to 10 minutes if you insist. But I would want to know how much waste time that produces.

questions.question: In the Maturation Pipeline's in-game acceptance stage, scripts give a pass or fail on each locked bar of a mod version, and separately an agent explores and takes screenshots before your live walk. There are two games: Archmagi (yours) and SteveDesktop (the unattended test machine, where 85 of 261 jobs died before judging anything from 11-06 to 11-14, mostly from machine and game faults). picked.label: Whichever game is free
picked.description: Why: get verdicts soonest and lean less on a faulty machine. Buys speed when SteveDesktop is down or busy. Costs: verdicts and exploring compete for Archmagi, so your sittings can wait on a test run. Slightly less to build, more to schedule.

questions.question: After a mod version passes, something must notice if a later change breaks it. Today SteveDesktop's 'guard' jobs re-run every mod's tests on a rotating schedule, changed or not. picked.label: On change, built later
picked.description: Why: nothing has passed yet, so there is nothing to guard today. Buys the right design without building it early; the schedule carries on meanwhile. GelatinousSlime is a universal living-body biome: the colony can take food, building material and poison relief from the same slime that absorbs unprotected people and can ultimately dissolve them. Native resistant life shares the body with outsiders already being absorbed; becoming slimified does not itself make a creature hostile. A chosen gene makes the bargain deliberate: select it from the archive, locate and extract its current with a handheld seeker, then inject a perishable dose that also brings an unwanted gene and a lasting social cost. The recipient falls into a coma and faces accelerated absorption unless a friend administers the toxic antidote in time. Ordinary exposure has its own slower course. Early ordinary film recedes away from slime ground; later film persists in ordinary country, so drying country or antidote provides the established way out. The giant Titanoslime engulfs and digests prey and grows permanently by default; a harvested, short-lived piece becomes a dangerous thrown bioweapon, including to nearby allies, and serves the campaign’s sealed-vault use. Expensive archive technology can return a dead person from their last recorded touch, while the colony’s later lives and relationships remain real. The player can use and survive this body, but its gifts carry readable, actionable consequences. Review: design/concepts/GelatinousSlime/stage1_review.json. text: BINDING ON THE ENTRY STANDARD AND MODLEDGER (~10:12 PM PST 2026-11-15). (1) No unlimited provenance: a wrong value is corrected with the right value and at most one sentence of why, only when the why matters to understanding; no essay on its wrongness. (2) Drain: an entry shown useless or wrong can be retracted (one short event naming it) so views, packet and search index no longer show it, and a dispatcher-only compaction physically removes retracted and corrected-away entries from the working shards; git history is the only archive. This narrows the spec's 'nothing is ever edited or deleted' and the NOT_APPEND lint: compaction is the one authorized non-append commit. Conductor's reconciliation of 'grows monotonically' with 'drain': the mod's state only moves forward; the file need not keep dead weight.
ownerSaid: Also we must resist unlimited provenance. If a wrong number is found fix it, don't document every aspect of its wrongness unless it matters to understanding. There must also be a way to drain items if they are shown to be useless or wrong.

text: card 1
byCard: What should a biome mod's first version (0.1.0) be allowed to contain → Land, life, one signature

questions.question: Measured tonight: the Designer has no rule for how big a first version may be. Leaning Scrub locked with 64 passing bars, 60 of them provable only in the live game, and the six held biome concepts list 44 to 86 capabilities each. What should a biome mod's first version (0.1.0) be allowed to contain?

picked.label: Land, life, one signature (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: the smallest biome that still feels like itself is the one that can pass. Terrain, plants, animals, weather, plus exactly ONE signature mechanic; everything else moves out. Cost: biomes arrive plainer, and the Designer may pick the wrong signature (you can swap it). Recommended: it is the only option with a hard edge.

others: A bar budget, no content rule

text: card 2
byCard: Default fate of an extra ruled out of the first version, and its code → Next version, switched off

questions.question: Some extras are already coded (rituals, small custom details). When the upgraded Designer rules one out of the first version, what should be the default fate of that extra and its code?

picked.label: Next version, switched off (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: you said 'at minimum next version'. The extra is written up for the next version and its code is turned off, so it cannot break a bar. Cost: a small build job per extra, and idle code can rot. Recommended: nothing is lost and nothing untested runs.

text: card 4
byCard: What should gate a cleansed design → One whole-mod check instead (of the cold-reader exam and the coverage judge)

questions.question: After writing, a design must pass two checkers today: a cold-reader exam (fresh agents judge 10 or more play situations from the bars alone) and a coverage judge (a fresh agent checks every capability has a test scene). The judge halted Contagion with 25 refusals and was stopped on Pyrelands by the 'nothing could ever pass' alarm; neither caught tonight's conflicting bars. What should gate a cleansed design?

picked.label: One whole-mod check instead (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: aim at what actually hurt. One fresh reviewer hunts bars that conflict, promised mechanics with no spec, scenes with the main mechanic off, and tuning numbers; one round of fixes, then lock. Cost: new and unproven; loses the capability-by-capability scene check. Recommended: the old gates missed all four.

others: Keep the gates as they are

questions.question: The blind checker (the judge that grades a builder's proof as PASS, WEAK, FAIL or UNMEASURED) today treats a WEAK verdict as PASS when the judge cannot say what strong proof would look like or what the weak proof lets through. picked.label: Adopt the four rules (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: few rules you can read and tune, each with one dial. Buys: prompt text plus two small fixes, undone by reverting one commit. Costs: with one full inspection, what the first look misses reaches play; unproven until recalibrated and one mod runs. Recommended: it is the smallest change that stops the repeat looks.

byCard: Void spend → Does not count (Recommended); Live runs → Each of these should be specific commands. "Stop work immediately and write where you are." questions.question: A "void" run is one that died of a system fault, was stopped by us, or that you declare should not count; under the new design it never spends a trial, look or cycle. Each stage also has a spend ceiling (about 25M weighted tokens) that pauses a mod when reached. The tokens a void run burnt are real. Should a void run's spend count toward that stage ceiling?

picked.label: Does not count (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: a ceiling should measure what the mod cost on its merits. Buys: no mod is paused by our own faults or stops. Costs: a fault loop could burn tokens unseen by the ceiling; a separate system-fault alarm must catch it. Recommended: it matches your rule that system failures never charge the mod.

questions.question: The new one-line command turns work off for everything, one mod, one stage or one item. New launches stop at once in every case. Today, stopping Graffiti's running work took a separate manual kill, while runs that are killed lose whatever they had not yet saved. What should turning something off do, by default, to runs that are already running?
questions.answer: Each of these should be specific commands. "Stop work immediately and write where you are." "Stop work at the next easy spot and write where you are." "STOP NOW without write." Defaults for the system are nice, sure... should be Stop work at the next easy spot and write where you are" should be the default always. But we shouldn't rely on defaults. The agent should be precise in its instruction and use the right option. We don't need to prethink this.

Strike a balance.; Old docs → I think we need to delete them, but man do I feel anxiety. There's a lot of beautiful creation in there. But yes, let's do this. And let's do it carefully. We will need artifacts that let us deeply see what was chosen, what was lost, and why. Possibly even different choices to make as we work together, ok?; Scope moves → Move it, list every move (Recommended); Judge order → I posted questions for this item already present and waiting for you
ownerSaid: PLEASE see them through the lens of Utinni. We're not optimizing these things for long-term play in a normal Rimworld game. They are going to be visited by a huge ship on the run descending from the sky crewed by hilarious, bizarre Jawa way in over their head. ESPECIALLY for 0.1.0 and even 0.2.0 this should be the overriding priority. And that ship is LEAVING soon... it has to. They are Empire-pursued by scenario design, so anything that takes seasons to observe will simply be missed. We need to FIX THE ONES WE HAVE. That even includes the old definition docs we originally wrote for the biomes. Let's rewrite them all and let git be provenance. I would say keep the DROP/1/2 decision a LITTLE open.

text: OWNER 2026-11-18 about 4:05 PM PST, two inputs for the consolidation pass after the second readers: (1) DARK is measured, not ruled: from the tidally locked planet and the canonical map (sun angle per tile); the Abyss's supernatural dark is its own thing. HIDDEN is a separate property (canopy, steam, fog, rock, water). Conductor's proposed default, to confirm at the theme sitting: ordinary measured dark = one step, each kind of cover = one step, only the Abyss's dark pauses the search. So every 'does X count as full dark' question in the designs is answered by measurement plus this rule. text: DESIGN DECISION 2026-11-18 6:40 PM PST. Nobody edits the exam's control copy by hand. A paraphrase of the removed leaf's rule is stripped by the program: exam-control <dir> --leaf <id> --strip "<phrase>" (repeatable; exam_control(d, leaf, strip=[...])), in whole units only: each sheet.md line holding the phrase is dropped, each list entry holding it is dropped, each other string value holding it becomes exactly "(removed)" (case and spacing aside). A phrase found in a retained leaf's id or experience is refused: two leaves then state one rule, so pick another core leaf for the control or return to stage 3. copy.json records the phrases under "strip"; control_copy_errors regenerates the copy from the current tree plus that list and refuses any difference. EVIDENCE [measured, 8 control copies under design/concepts regenerated and diffed at b28e0d697]: 4 carry no hand strip (Contagion, FeverWood, LeaningScrub, Pyrelands); Graffiti and GelatinousSlime cut a phrase from inside a sheet line and from tree key advisory; Stillsand cut a phrase from inside retained leaf scene_observer.tier_reason; Cauldron's copy is from an older tree (already refused). So real strips are phrase cuts inside a line, which is exactly the edit that can delete 'not'; none was checked. RULES OUT: byte-equal retained leaves with hand strips elsewhere (a hand cut in the sheet or a non-leaf value can still reverse a sentence); deletion-only (deleting 'not' reverses); a reviewer approving each edit (a paid judge where a comparison does it); sentence-level strips (no evidence yet that a whole-value strip costs a control its discrimination; add later only with a measured case). SMALLEST BUILD: exam_control takes strip; copy.json records it; control_copy_errors regenerates and compares tree.json and sheet.md; roles/designer_exam.md step 5 and its last bullet say 'name the phrase to the program, never edit the copy'. The four existing hand-stripped copies must not be newly refused where they pass today: the build writes their tree.json+sheet.md content hashes to a one-time allowlist, and the builder shows control_copy_errors over the 8 real dirs is the same before and after. This ticket IS the build ticket. Acceptance test extended to the rule: python3 src/RimMandrake/rimflow/acceptance/control_copy_retained_rules_accept.py, 19 checks, 13 red on b28e0d697 (watched), 1 green there (the generated copy passes); 5 more run only once strip exists.

It costs about 4.6 million weighted tokens on a full day, 25 to 29 runs. 56% of that pays for the start package: the rule files, memory file and skill list each run loads before it reads its alarm. About half of the package has nothing to do with Operations. Each pick below makes one run cheaper. (Hard to read? Type STE, Binding or Both for a rewrite.) Which of these do I build?
questions.answer: Slim the start package (Recommended), Trim waste inside a run, Sonnet for follow-ups only, "If we escalate to (4) then we would likely give Sonnet Escalation: recognize something is fishy, so call out Opus to continue."

picked.label: Slim the start package (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: it cuts every run, on either model, and the same change can later go to every role. Removes the skill list, your personal rule file and the memory file from Operations runs, and stops telling them they are the Conductor. Saves about 1.2 to 1.8M a day [guess]. Cost: small build, 1 day test; a rule only in your personal file is no longer seen.

questions.his_words: Slim the start package (Recommended), Trim waste inside a run, Sonnet for follow-ups only, "If we escalate to (4) then we would likely give Sonnet Escalation: recognize something is fishy, so call out Opus to continue."

questions.question: [owner-asked] The second way to cut Operations is fewer runs. It was planned as about 10 runs a day and makes 25 to 29. Of 105 runs, about 13 landed a real fix; 57 only wrote a note, and those 57 were 38% of the spend. Two causes: a bug that treats "the plan is one hour older" as news and starts a follow-up run each hour, and five alarms that always get the same "nothing to fix" answer (unclaimed SteveDesktop incident, low lukas runway, standing wrap-up debris, idle pipeline, scratch dirt). Which of these do I build?
questions.answer: Fix the news bug (Recommended), Program answers 5 repeat alarms, Program follows open incidents

picked.label: Fix the news bug (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: 11 of 42 follow-up launches were set off by a reading that only aged. A reading that just gets older stops counting as news. Saves about 0.5 to 1.0M a day [guess]. Cost: small build with its test; a real jump in those readings is caught one step later. Works well with the program-answers pick: together they are the plan the analysis advises.

picked.label: Program answers 5 repeat alarms
picked.description: Why: a sixth look at those five alarms found something new 0 times. A program writes the same note the agent wrote, and calls the agent only when a reading leaves a stated range. Saves about 0.5 to 0.9M a day [guess]. Cost: small to medium build, 2 days test; a later look that would have found something is lost.

picked.label: Program follows open incidents
picked.description: Why: the biggest cut in run count. A program re-reads each open incident's numbers and calls the agent only when one crosses a stated line; one deep Opus run a day stays. Saves about 1.0 to 1.8M a day [guess, low confidence]; it includes the news-bug fix. Cost: medium build, 2 to 3 days test; each incident plan needs a line a program can check.

questions.question: [owner-asked] One more item saves no tokens. On Nov 17 the fleet stopped twice when the lukas account hit its floor. The page showed "runway 10" for the next account, because runway is computed from each account's own burn, and an unused account burns nothing. No reading said how long the next account would last once the fleet moved onto it. Only two choices here: the reading is built or it is not. Do I build that reading and a short-window burn alarm?

picked.label: Build it now (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: it is the reading that would have warned of both Nov 17 stops, and it is a program, so it costs no tokens to run. Applies the fleet's measured burn to each account it could move to, and alarms on a fast burn inside a few hours. Cost: one detached build run and its tests.

questions.question: [owner-asked] One more item saves no tokens. On Nov 17 the fleet stopped twice when the lukas account hit its floor. The page showed "runway 10" for the next account, because runway is computed from each account's own burn, and an unused account burns nothing. questions.question: Thu Nov 19, 5:54 PM PST. Four choices finish the review method. Two rows I will add without asking, because you already stated them: a finding is significant when it is measured, or predicted with a concrete case (this input, this wrong result), to break a promise or cause a failure; and a ticket must cite a broken promise or a failure, one ticket per source event. picked.label: The reviewer, on the spot (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: the finder holds the whole file and its own reasoning, as in the old loop you found fast and good. The reviewer writes a new test, sees it fail, fixes, sees it pass. Costs: the same agent finds and fixes, so the test is the only independent check. Recommended: it removes the ticket handoff that loses context.

questions.question: After a significant finding is fixed, the old loop left the file dirty until a fresh blind reader passed it. Your rule today says one round. Measured: on quiet mod files the reread found 0 new bugs; on fast-changing pipeline files 8 of 11 and 9 of 15 later claims pointed at lines the last fix had just written, mostly polish. Under today's rule polish is noted and not fixed. What checks a fix?
questions.answer: (2) Precisely one, yes. If it too finds a significant change and fixes it, the file is flagged but left alone. Flagged files are examined to see if we need to change the definition of significant or there is a real instability, but this is done infrequently, say weekly or so.

picked.label: One blind reread of the fix
picked.description: Why: the old way, which caught fixes that broke something else. A fresh reader reads the fixed file once; significant findings are fixed, minor ones noted, then it ends with no third read. Buys: a second mind. Costs: a second run per fixed file, and fresh fix lines draw the most claims.

title: Enact his ruling of 2026-11-19 evening: touching code has a cost, so every fixer, reviewer, judge and pipeline monitor justifies the touch; if you see it, do it; a real chance of voiding a run is always vital. Same card: a stopping level in every judging brief
ownerSaid: We JUST changed standing orders across this whole project. Please be advised and make the changes. This is standing policy for all FIXERS that receive a ticket (is it really fixing something that anyone would care about?), REVIEWERS/JUDGES (is this a significant comment/change), and pipeline monitors (are these tickets impactful, meaningful, and worthy of action)? Basically we're introducing a new concept: TOUCHING code has a COST. It's DANGEROUS at a low noise-level, so you must justify doing it, and that includes old tickets that didn't justify why. So by that criteria, yes! Go and "judge" the tickets now to see if they are "worthy" the risk of their repair. Obviously the ones with failing tests are a go. Maybe you can group them together to repair them in a single context more cheaply, that would be welcome. I would also like to introduce the idea that ANYONE can be a fixer. If a ticket adjudicant in THIS VERY EXERCISE picks up a ticket and can clearly see "yes this is valid and I can even see how to easily fix it"... PLEASE DO. Don't make someone else go read everything and decide yet again... Just please do it! This is the "If you see it, do it" rule. In essence, you have to have evidence that you should NOT do so. The assumption to just "set a ticket down for someone else later with 'fixer' on their forehead" is false... the fixer is you unless you can prove you don't have the resources or currently have other responsibilities that prevent you from investing. Feel free to push back, but this seems very important and is very much in the spirit of the old successful Foundry process, even now. Vital: OF COURSE you do, no debate. Any real chance of voiding a run is catastrophic.

ownerSaid: the white hazy blocks inside the pit I do not think were "TheForge" but yes the geysers were. I didn't mind the steam so much, but the meaningless pale region around steamgeysers I definitely did. And Biome mechanics in general do NOT stay confined to the biome of origin: they are universal, but that biome depends on them, showcases them, or has the materials or sources to make them or make them shine. For example, the Stillshade has nothing "special" about its long shadows and intense sun exposure effects: those should be planet-wide. But the Stillshade showcases them with a unique biome adaptation to them. Make sense? The Rot features a living floor covering that heats rooms and keeps life alive in the cold through food consumption. It works anywhere, but it's native to the Rot and must be tended and carried elsewhere. We should also make it die in direct Sun exposure to explain why the Rot hasn't spread over the whole surface. Please take the GENERAL lessons in this message as guiding principles for the whole game, Baroque Biomes, etc. But then take my specific examples and enact them as well in specific tickets. If there are conflicting rulings, please let's review them right now and correct them to avoid ambiguity. If there are specific conflicts (current mechanics that don't honor these principles) let's also rule on them. But remember: Form first, Specifics later, ok? This is a big request I understand, so give it the resources it needs. And I think it's time we start some kind of Guiding Principles document for this entire project, similar to the LEXICON.md but for meta-rules that should always apply beyond any particular mod or biome. In fact, I'd like you to file a ticket with Lodestar to create GUIDING_PRINCIPLES.md as a basic aspect of all Lodestar-tracked projects from now on (and retroactively derive and add them interactively with the user) as part of the birth-certificate process and to evolve as the project morphs forward. questions.question: This is the second card on your new principles file, which says what is always true of the game. Two entries are ruled: a mechanic reads conditions and never the biome; a visible effect with no meaning is removed. These four lines are proposed, and I think each is worth adopting. An adopted line binds every designer and judge agent from today. (Hard to read? Type STE, Binding or Both for a rewrite.) Which of these four proposed lines do you adopt as principles?
questions.answer: A limit lives in the world, An effect that implies harm is true, Mechanics justify their combined load, "No offline testing, we test only where the mechanics matter. And many mechanics WILL effectively only be in a single biome (e.g. tar mechanics don't matter where there are no tar pits... unless the players bring tar somewhere of course). We don't test outside the source biome at this time. Perhaps in future versions, but not now. I also don't want to say it is FORBIDDEN to have a specific biome mechanic, that is not how the rule should be written. I mean to say all of the biome specifics mechanics so far stated are per condition, not by some magic in a specific biome. The Abyss is a good example. There are no tiny particulates on other maps for the mechanic to engage with, so it will never be seen there. If we made a creature with those tiny particulates present, it should still work as in the Abyss... but we're not doing that right now. Make sense? If a mechanic is a heavy load even when not \"active\" in all other biomes, we may make the call to simply not load it outside the parent biome... I want to preserve that capability. But that should be the exception, not the rule, and stated. "

picked.label: A limit lives in the world
picked.description: Why: a mechanic is held back by things the player can fight (a roof beats sunlight, farming feeds the Rot), never by a hidden code limit. Buys limits that are gameplay. Costs design work: each spreading mechanic needs a real in-world brake, and a thriving transplant counts as good play.

text: STEWARD DECISION (visit 6 road back, delegated, Evidence-for-Ask): the design ruling is taken, so the fix is known. Design §4.1 (design/RimMandrake/flowworks_bridges_design_2026-10-17.md) gives the solid deck a LOW chance and the grated deck a HIGH chance. The intent is that the solid deck is the shield and the grate is the hazard. A per-60-tick chance of 0.35 saturates over one burn, so 'low' is lost. The answer: the solid deck's low chance applies per burn exposure, not per effects check. The chance that a solid-deck rider catches fire over one inferno burn stays at or below today's low onCover figure (0.4). A grated rider keeps the high chance per check. The mechanism (one roll per exposure, or a per-check chance scaled to the burn length) is the fixer's choice. A full shield was not chosen, because §4.1 says 'low', not 'none'. No bar changes: hung_bridge_spans and inv_bridges keep their words. RED FIRST: add a C# selftest case in src/RimMandrake/FlowWorks/Source/SelfTest/FuelFireChecks.cs. The case computes 1-(1-p)^n for a solid-deck rider over one burn's effects checks and asserts <= 0.4. It is red at 65c45b6e98 (0.35 per check). Fix RM_FuelFireMath / RM_LiquidFire.cs:550 (and the :634 site through RM_FireMath.AttachChance, if it is on the same path). Green: selftest_flowworks_stock.py --only FuelFire_inferno_solid_deck_*. Then record the live check UNRUN for Stage 6: sc_hung_bridge GRATE_fire_burns_people_above, three PASS in a row (maturation.py unrun). The fixer also checks that the GRATE row's verdict is not chance under the new rule. With per-burn solid <= 0.4 and grate near 1, the margin must hold over the scene's rider count. If the margin is too thin, raise the rider count. Do not loosen the row.

text: His direction for the coordination plan: the pipeline takes over more, knows when it needs a human and when it does not; do not revert toward Bench and Foundry (the human as the pipeline); mods keep their own state; everything outside a mod goes in ONE list, one place to write and one place to close. ownerSaid: Ok, as far as the whole old pipeline vs new. Foundry and Bench WORKED. But they were using the human as many aspects of what we now call the Maturation Pipeline manually. Because the pipeline wasn't working for a bit, we seem to be reverting back towards Bench and Foundry. But that's the wrong way, making it more and more efficient to ask me to judge things via a walk and through constant talking. Instead we need to improve the pipeline to take over more of these capabilities in a semi automated fashion, know when it's in trouble and needs a human, but also recognize when it's not. THAT's the motivation for all the modifications to the pipeline. Not just "constantly shifting the pipeline" as seems to be the interpretation of GPT and others when they review. We're still trying to make a pipeline that can handle this stuff, and that's ok, as long as we're converging. What we've found is that we're great at capturing needed work that's generated by the pipeline itself, but poor at capturing and integrating and pursuing additional work made when you consult the human, or that questions the pipeline itself. Conversely, when we focus on that, we tend to start dropping the routine work of the pipeline. It seems to be a focus of attention problem. That's why I thought it might help to have a ledger that can reliably be checked instead of the "25 places" you suggested. I still don't quite understand why that wouldn't help. one place to write things down, one place to close them... seems useful. It's ok to have mods track their own state, that I understand. The point of agents and pipelines. But anything outside that context seems like it should then go into a single "holds everything else" list to me. Push back if you wish, but explain why please. Incorporate this argument into your analysis, correct my mistakes, and advance our plans please.

title: FlowWorks: melee across a pit's edge works only when the attacker could reach, by the same criterion as climbing: a pawn that cannot climb out cannot melee out; a pawn that could not climb in cannot melee down in. Body size decides, so a large creature reaches farther and the result can be one-way. Replaces the blanket 'No melee across a pit's edge' rule of 4e01c63a3f5b; the Mod Settings switch stays a plain on/off, default on
ownerSaid: It's a simple ruling. Melee across a pit ledge (in to out or out to in) should only work if the creature could feasibly reach out. But that is the same criteria as being able to climb out. So anything that can't climb out also cannot melee attack out. Same for melee attacking "down" into the pit. If you couldn't climb in you can't melee attack in. So a very large creature can attack farther down a pit than a little one. And there can be cases where a large creature can attack a smaller one but not vice versa. It's all quite sensible.

ownerSaid: YES! Stochastic event testing requires the changes you pose. 0) We need to define three things to make this work. A: deterministic test (should always be reliably testable, the standard default, what we assume today). B: Stochastic test (testing a reliable capability with many input variables that make the test's outcome unreliable, thus requiring looking for evidence-of-success rather than guaranteed reproducable success on demand. Only justified due to large numbers of unreliable environmental variables or a capability that itself stochastic in yield/production by intention) C: Intermittent test (the test itself is deterministic, but it's seeking an intermittent bug that only occasionally manifests due to complex environments or unknown nature, thus requiring looking for evidence-of-failure amidst repeated apparent successes). We need to explicitly tag tests for their intention, so they can be repeated and judged appropriately. Approved explicitly: 1) Force the situation ALWAYS if possible, there are too many variables to control otherwise. 2) Broaden this definition of detection/success/failure to handle A, B, and C cases explicitly. 3) Required to handle case B. 4) Correct, a detected failed environment is not a mod failure and may or may not indicate a testing apparatus failure, depending on the level of our own control. Each time a failed environmental variable is identified, the testing environment (number of loaded mods, calm testing environment definition, use of or creation of new BRIDGE capabilities to remove the influences) should be explored and exercised if possible. There will likely always be some residual testing influences, but let's get VERY creative in trying to remove them to preserve sanity and not burn all our tokens on repeating large expensive test suites with low yields even if the mod is 100% correct. Push back and question card me, expand this prompt to make it excellent. This is a VITAL upgrade, immediate priority, work with me Fable right now! Then we send it to GPT afterwards for deep review, skeptical breakdown, and fix improvements, and finally work together on the final token-efficient simple bearing language version.

questions.question: One point from my pushback is still open. In kind B (a stochastic test, judged by evidence of success) you said any demonstration of success may be as good as we get. I agree, with one hole: a failed run that nobody can class as an environment fault or a test-apparatus fault. If such a run simply does not count, a real mod bug that shows one time in five disappears. The draft's answer: every failed run of a kind B test is read once and classed; an unclassed failure is recorded; if the same unclassed failure is seen a second time, it opens a kind C hunt (the temporary hunt for an intermittent bug). You said kind C opens 'after having been seen once or twice'. What should happen to a kind B failure that nobody can explain?
questions.answer: (1) repeated unexplained failures indicate deeper investigation is required, yes. I would also like to suggest that a Hunt be communicated to the Conductor as an opportunity for Fable Rescue (or at least to be included in such a rescue if it is called later), or the Conductor may choose to look and give a second perspective with its different context to assist. It should not be a silent conversion to a Hunt. It's a big deal in a mod's testing to need this.

picked.label: Record it; a second sighting opens a hunt (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: one odd run is usually noise, two alike is a pattern. Buys: no hunt on a single fluke; a repeating bug cannot hide behind the B tag. Costs: one short read per failed run, and the records must be comparable so a second sighting is recognised. Recommended: cheapest rule that still catches a real bug.

text: Agreement reached on Bridge 2's shape; no YAML scene language; scan Inhabited and consider it for the bridge rebuild.
ownerSaid: We are in agreement. I am totally OK with building more functionality into BRIDGE to offer yet more capabilities for PYTHON to select at build-time, not for the agent to select during play-time. In fact I'm fairly certain we DO need more, I like your per-tick capture strategy quite a bit. We are in agreement on these points for sure. I hope you don't think I'm pushing back too strongly on that. Perhaps we should come together to make sure we're reviewing what we agree and disagree on? I want to help, not hinder this improvement phase. I think we need it. And no, I don't think we need a YAML scene language. We already have something called "Inhabited" that was going to be something like that to inject real-agent-based content during gameplay (built but not to modern spec) to vastly enrich the game beyond what we could ever put in Python (actual LLM calls to improve raids, character behavior, plot decisions, etc). Then we invented the Python-based BRIDGE for testing, and I realized likely that would actually overtake Inhabited (or perhaps already did, I don't remember where that mod state ended up right now). We certainly don't need yet another one. Take a look at it actually, you should consider it now. We DO one day really want a live-game BRIDGE use function to inject awesome "improve the tile map" capability, "improve the raid" capability, etc. And it might inform this BRIDGE rebuild too. Scan for Inhabited.

text: He settles the open points and asks for the design now: he reads one-page contracts; receipts yes; design from what has needed it, extended only where evidence points; unused bridge capabilities are to be published so agents use them; a struggle in Python is the signal for a better hands function; deep in-game access is wanted; Inhabited is built toward mindfully, after the four current mods.
ownerSaid: I feel we are informed enough by now to make a beautiful design right now. It is strongly informed by what has needed it so far, and we can extend that into the future a bit. I agree we shouldn't pre-design far into the future, only where the evidence seems to point. Especially Bridge capabilities that aren't being used are ripe fodder to figure out how to publish that in a way agents use better. Or if we're struggling to build what we need in Python but can't seem to and want to put it in C# suggests better "hands" functions in the BRIDGE. And as the evidence suggests, new BRIDGE capabilities (especially deep in-game access like hidden variable reads, per-tick captures and actions, etc.) make complete sense. HEY, I never saw you respond to my idea for modifying variables live, in-game, like the RIMMSQOL mod. I am willing to read one-page contracts, yes. YES, Python entry point receipts are excellent. Yes, we can build toward Inhabited mindfully, though we're not optimizing that yet. But if there's something with weak testing value now and strong value for Inhabited, it is worth it. Inhabited WILL be built into this game, yes, though I have never exposed it to the modern pipeline yet. If you feel it would be advantageous to build toward it now, we can after these four current mods.

Then the machine pauses, then it switches accounts, and the switch stops every Claude process. The pause must be long enough for runs to save, and short enough that the account does not reach 0%, where every window errors and you cannot talk to a seat. The meter shows whole percents, so a reading of 1% can mean 0.5% is left, which is about 7 minutes from zero at that rate. picked.label: Sized from the burn rate (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: the safe pause depends on how many runs are spending. The machine reads the current burn and pauses for a fifth of the time to zero, 3 minutes at most. Buys: safe at any load, long when few runs are live. Costs: one more calculation that can be wrong if the burn reading is stale. Recommended: it is the only option that holds your under-10% chance at every load.

No switch happens because another account stands earlier in a list or an alphabet. Order only answers one question: when the live account is finished, which account is next. (2) A switch is costly (every window restarts, live runs are interrupted), so the plan makes the fewest switches that use the allowance that would otherwise be lost. (3) New runs are refused only when the live account is at its own warning line, never for a switch that is a preference. (4) A reset that would erase allowance is a reason to plan ahead (use that account before its reset), but the plan weighs it against the cost of a switch and says its reasoning in one line. (5) State comes from fresh measurements, never from a marker. Today's faults are all census rows: the stale marker on steven; a forecast that ignored markers and so disagreed with the real pick; a preference switch that drained lukas at 18 percent left and refused new runs for 49 minutes; a plan change that needed a JSON hand edit, a publish and a pull into the timer's clone, with a HOLD file written by hand 6 seconds before a timer pass to stop a wrong switch; a stop order and its undo that crossed. Also on this item: the reset-day rule and the 25 percent Codex leave line. The stages after design stand as briefed: comparison, code with a test per promise and per census row, planted faults, shadow and replay; the cut-over is the Conductor's act.

Redesign it to avoid ALL the mistakes we keep encountering! This is ridiculous. Please build something that behaves as a human might make their own decisions... such as to stay on an account and drain it without incurring additional switches because of alphabetical order or arbitrary list order...

text: MORE OF THE ORDER, for the design (the owner's words follow). (A) BURN MODE: when an account is near its reset with allowance that the reset would erase, the plan says so as a state that other programs read, and work that can use that allowance fully and usefully is given priority (more helper slots, the heavy queued work first, Codex work when the account is Codex). Design what enters Burn Mode (allowance left, time to reset, the burn that would be needed against the burn that is measured), what it changes and through which existing program (the helper allocator and the pipelines own concurrency and order; this tool publishes the state and the target burn, as it publishes the pool today), what ends it, and what it must never do (start worthless work to hit a number; cross a leave line that is not lifted; overload the machine: today the load reached 41 to 64 and tests went flaky). (B) THE MEASURES, in his order: first, allowance wasted (points that a reset erased unused, per account and week) and work wasted by switching (runs interrupted or restarted by a switch, windows restarted); then the speed, ease and responsiveness of a decision (Python, no model call); then how clearly the tool answers three questions: what happens now, what happens next, and what happens if I say this. The tool reports the first two measures itself, from its own log, for each past week and as a forecast for the current plan; the replay of stage 5 scores the old engine and the new plan on the same two measures, and that comparison decides stage 3.
ownerSaid: I would also like to build into it a "Burn Mode" concept where, when an account is near refresh, tasks that can benefit and load it fully are prioritized so we optimize token usage. Minimizing token wastage (as well as wasted work from switching) should be two of the primary metrics. Then there should be the speed, ease, and responsiveness of making decisions (i.e. python not LLM) and the clarity of knowing "what will happen now, next, and if I say this?"

title: Build the Temporary Work Bundle Monitor: a daily program that measures the share of work through Work Bundles against single-ticket runs on both pipelines, the weighted tokens per ticket that stays closed three days, and every set-down and backward stage move judged for sincerity by an LLM; one report a day to the Conductor with evidence, three repairs and one recommendation; a section on the Maturation Pipeline page and a digest line; timer rm-work-bundle-monitor.timer. Acceptance test: the selftests of design/specs/2026-11-25-temporary-work-bundle-monitor/boundary.md red on planted faults and green after; one real report of 2026-11-25; the close carries its live promise
byCard: Monitor acts → Wake the Conductor to decide; Sincerity → An LLM reads every one (Recommended); Efficiency → Tokens per ticket that stays closed (Recommended); Where shown → Pipeline page plus a digest line (Recommended)

questions.question: The daily monitor is a program that reads the last day's run records. It reports three things. First: how much work went through Work Bundles (one run that fixes many tickets of one mod or subsystem in one context) against single-ticket runs. Second: how efficient each kind was. Third: how often a run set work down, or a mod moved back a stage, without a sincere attempt to fix in place. (Hard to read? Type STE, Binding or Both for a rewrite.) When the monitor finds a bad pattern, what should the monitor do with it?
questions.answer: (4) is acceptable here. We should call this explicitly the Temporary Work Bundle Monitor, because we're not intending to keep it longer than is necessary to evaluate this change to the pipeline. Its recommendations should go to you, Conductor, because you are Fable and much smarter and with a broader pipeline context. However, the monitor should absolutely have done its homework, provide evidence and measurements, and offer three options for repair with its recommendation made clear. This will hopefully reduce the amount of time you need to spend on it, and it's only one a day. If the Monitor continues to be useful as a more general Pipeline Monitor / Upgrade system, we should fold it instead into Operations in a more formal manner. Agreed?

picked.label: Wake the Conductor to decide
picked.description: Why: keep a judgment between finding and fix. Buys: I can reject a wrong diagnosis before anything changes. Costs: it needs my window each day, and the pipeline is supposed to run without it.

questions.question: Effort is the setting that tells a model how hard to think on each step: medium, high, xhigh or max. I measured the last three days of runs. On Archmagi: 707 Opus runs at high, 134 Sonnet runs at medium, 44 Fable runs at medium. On SteveDesktop: all 32 Opus runs at medium, because that machine lacked the setting (I fixed that at 11:40 AM PST for new runs). Our launchers pass no effort; each run takes whatever the machine's settings say. (Hard to read? Type STE, Binding or Both for a rewrite.) What effort should a run that builds or fixes start at?

picked.label: No medium anywhere
picked.description: Why: simplicity, one floor for everything. Buys: no run is ever under-thinking, and no rule to remember. Costs: searches, counts and bare judge calls also pay for high, where a test or a re-read catches mistakes cheaply anyway.

others: Keep medium first, raise on failure

questions.question: A worker is stuck when its fix failed once, or when the new ticket filer refuses its attempt to file the problem instead of fixing it. I tested one thing just now: resuming the same session at a higher effort keeps its prompt cache (a Sonnet session went medium to high to xhigh and re-wrote under 600 tokens each time), so 'try harder' in the same context is nearly free. Changing the model is different: it always re-writes the whole context (measured this morning: a median 566k weighted tokens to Opus, 1.2M to Fable). What should the pipeline do with a stuck worker?

picked.label: Effort up, then model up (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: use the nearly free step first. The pipeline resumes the same session one effort level higher. If still stuck, the worker writes its theories and readings to a note and a higher model starts fresh from that note. Only then does it reach me. Costs: new launcher code. Recommended: it matches the measured costs.

others: Keep rescue as a Conductor decision

questions.question: You see the Test Pilot (a Fable run that debugs one stuck item live, by experiment), the Fable Rescue (a Fable run sent in when ordinary runs fail on a mod) and the ordinary Work Bundle worker (an Opus run that builds, tests offline and tests live in one context) as one thing. I agree on what they do. The one real difference left is method: the Test Pilot writes its theories before it experiments and changes one thing per experiment, where a builder codes and retests. How should the role definitions change?

picked.label: One builder, three settings (Recommended)
picked.description: Why: one definition to maintain and no hand-off between roles. A single builder file; model, effort and scope are launch settings; the Test Pilot's experiment method becomes what any builder does once stuck. Costs: a rewrite of three role files and their launch paths. Recommended: the roles already differ only in settings.

questions.question: Fable is the top model tier, used for the Conductor window, the Test Pilot and rescues. I measured 44 Fable runs in three days at medium effort and one at xhigh.
